2.2.1.examLens: Classify data correctly (this decides every tool you pick later), keep population and sample straight, and handle simple probability rules.

worked.question: (a) Classify: time to answer a call; number of defects on a circuit board; a 1 to 5 satisfaction rating; pass/fail of a weld. (b) A 2% defective rate, 5 independent units: what is the probability that at least one is defective?
worked.solution:
(a) Time: continuous (ratio). Defects per board: discrete (count). Rating: discrete (ordinal). Weld: discrete (binary, nominal).
(b) 1 − (0.98)⁵ = 1 − 0.9039 = 0.0961, about 9.6%.

2.2.2.examLens: Compute a mean, standard deviation, and range by hand, identify skew from the mean and median, and avoid the calculator trap on standard deviation keys.

worked.question: Data: 12, 15, 11, 18, 14. Find the mean, median, range, and sample standard deviation.
worked.solution:
Sum = 70, so mean = 14. Sorted: 11, 12, 14, 15, 18, so median = 14. Range = 18 − 11 = 7.
Deviations: −2, 1, −3, 4, 0. Squares: 4, 1, 9, 16, 0, total 30. Sample variance = 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5. s = √7.5 = 2.74.
(Using the population formula would give √6 = 2.45, which is the wrong key for a sample.)

2.2.3.examLens: Find probabilities with z, use the Z table correctly, and interpret a normality test.

worked.question: A process is normal with mean 50 and σ = 4. (a) What fraction exceeds 56? (b) What fraction lies between 46 and 54? (c) A normality test gives p = 0.03. What do you conclude at α = 0.05?
worked.solution:
(a) z = (56 − 50) ÷ 4 = 1.5. P(Z above 1.5) = 1 − 0.93319 = 0.0668 (6.68%).
(b) z = ±1.0, so the area = 1 − 2 × 0.15866 = 0.6827 (68.3%).
(c) p = 0.03 ≤ 0.05, so there is evidence the data are not normal.

2.2.4.examLens: Pick the right chart for the question, and read what a chart is telling you.

worked.question: Pick the best chart: (a) comparing cycle times across three shifts; (b) checking whether the process drifted over the last 30 days; (c) testing whether temperature relates to defect rate; (d) deciding which defect type to attack first.

2.2.1.a.title: Continuous versus discrete data
2.2.1.a.html:
• Continuous (variable) data is measured and can take any value in a range, including decimals: time, weight, length, temperature.
  • Discrete (attribute) data is counted or classified: number of defects, pass/fail, yes/no, category.

Test: can you sensibly say "2.37"? If yes, it is continuous. A count of defects per unit is discrete even when the numbers get large.

2.2.1.b.title: Scales of measurement (NOIR)
2.2.1.b.html:
• Nominal: categories with no order (shift A, B, C).
  • Ordinal: ordered, but the gaps are not equal (satisfaction 1 to 5).
  • Interval: equal gaps, no true zero (temperature in °C).
  • Ratio: equal gaps and a true zero (weight, time, length).

2.2.1.c.title: Population versus sample
2.2.1.c.html:
• A population is everything you want to know about. Its summary values are parameters: μ (mean), σ (standard deviation), N (count).
  • A sample is the part you actually measure. Its summary values are statistics: x̄, s, n.

You use statistics to estimate parameters.

2.2.1.d.title: Probability rules
2.2.1.d.html:
• Addition: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). If A and B are mutually exclusive, the last term is zero.
  • Multiplication: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A). If A and B are independent, P(B | A) = P(B), so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • Conditional: P(B | A) = P(A and B) ÷ P(A).

Example: P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5. If independent, P(A and B) = 0.15 and P(A or B) = 0.3 + 0.5 − 0.15 = 0.65. If mutually exclusive, P(A and B) = 0 and P(A or B) = 0.8.

2.2.1.e.title: Independent versus mutually exclusive
2.2.1.e.html:
• Independent: one event does not change the probability of the other.
  • Mutually exclusive: the events cannot both happen.

These are not the same. Two mutually exclusive events (each with positive probability) are actually dependent, because if one occurs the other cannot.

2.2.1.f.title: Data collection plan
2.2.1.f.html: A written plan that says what will be measured (with an operational definition), how (instrument and method), who collects it, when and how often, how many (sample size), and where it is recorded. It also lists factors to record for stratification (shift, machine, product).

2.2.1.g.title: Classify the data type
2.2.1.g.html: Pass/fail is discrete. A measured length is continuous. A 1-to-5 rating is discrete, ordinal. Time to answer a call is continuous, ratio.

2.2.1.h.title: Complement rule, binomial and Poisson by hand
2.2.1.h.html:
• At least one: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).
  • Binomial: P(x) = nCx · pˣ · (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ, used for counts of defectives in n independent trials.
  • Poisson: P(x) = e^(−λ) · λˣ ÷ x!, used for counts of defects over a fixed opportunity.

Examples: with a 2% defective rate, P(at least one defective in 5 units) = 1 − 0.98⁵ = 1 − 0.9039 = 0.0961. Binomial P(exactly 1 in 5) = 5 × 0.02 × 0.98⁴ = 0.0922. Poisson with λ = 2: P(3) = e⁻² × 8 ÷ 6 = 0.1804.

2.2.2.a.title: Central tendency
2.2.2.a.html:
• Mean: the arithmetic average. Pulled by outliers.
  • Median: the middle value when sorted. Resistant to outliers.
  • Mode: the most frequent value.

2.2.2.b.title: Spread
2.2.2.b.html:
• Range: highest − lowest.
  • Variance: the average squared distance from the mean.
  • Standard deviation: the square root of variance, in the original units.
  • IQR (interquartile range): Q3 − Q1.

2.2.2.d.title: Standard deviation
2.2.2.d.html:
s = √[ Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1) ]. A sample divides by n − 1. A population divides by N.
Example: data 4, 8, 6, 5, 7. Mean = 6. Deviations: −2, 2, 0, −1, 1. Squares: 4, 4, 0, 1, 1, total 10. Sample variance = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5, so s = 1.58. Population σ = √(10 ÷ 5) = 1.41.

2.2.2.e.title: Skew
2.2.2.e.html:
• Right (positive) skew: a long tail to the right. Mean > median > mode.
  • Left (negative) skew: a long tail to the left. Mean below median, which is below mode.
  • Symmetric: mean ≈ median ≈ mode.

2.2.2.f.title: Percentiles and quartiles
2.2.2.f.html: The 25th percentile (Q1), 50th (median), and 75th (Q3) split the sorted data into four equal parts. An outlier is commonly flagged if it lies beyond 1.5 × IQR from the quartiles.

2.2.2.g.title: Within versus overall variation
2.2.2.g.html:
• Within-subgroup (short-term) variation comes from the common causes inside a subgroup.
  • Overall (long-term) variation also includes shifts between subgroups.

This is the root of the difference between Cp/Cpk (within) and Pp/Ppk (overall) in 2.4.1.

2.2.2.h.title: Coefficient of variation
2.2.2.h.html: Extension, glossary only. CV = s ÷ x̄. It compares spread across data sets with different means. Low exam yield.

2.2.2.i.title: Skew from the mean and median
2.2.2.i.html: Given mean 52 and median 48, the mean is higher, so the data are right-skewed. Outliers pull the mean, not the median.

2.2.2.j.title: Variances add, standard deviations do not
2.2.2.j.html:
For independent variables, σ²(total) = σ²₁ + σ²₂. This also applies to differences.
Example: two stacked parts with σ₁ = 3 and σ₂ = 4. σ(total) = √(9 + 16) = 5, not 7.

2.2.2.k.title: Reference-sheet extras
2.2.2.k.html:
• Weighted mean = Σ(w · x) ÷ Σw.
  • Mean of grouped data = Σ(f · X) ÷ n, with X = class midpoint and f = frequency.
  • Mean deviation = Σ|X − x̄| ÷ n.
  • s = σ(n) × √[n ÷ (n − 1)], linking the "divide by n" and "divide by n − 1" forms.

Examples: scores 80 (weight 3) and 90 (weight 2) give (240 + 180) ÷ 5 = 84. Classes with midpoints 10, 20, 30 and frequencies 5, 10, 5 give (50 + 200 + 150) ÷ 20 = 20. Mean deviation for 4, 8, 6, 5, 7 = (2 + 2 + 0 + 1 + 1) ÷ 5 = 1.2.
Calculator trap: most calculators have two standard deviation keys, one for the population (σn) and one for the sample (s, n − 1). Use the sample key for sample data.

2.2.3.a.title: The normal curve
2.2.3.a.html: A symmetric bell curve defined by its mean μ and standard deviation σ. Mean, median, and mode coincide. The total area under the curve is 1.

2.2.3.b.title: The empirical rule
2.2.3.b.html:
• μ ± 1σ contains about 68%
  • μ ± 2σ contains about 95%
  • μ ± 3σ contains about 99.7%

2.2.3.c.title: The z-score
2.2.3.c.html: z = (x − μ) ÷ σ tells you how many standard deviations a value is from the mean. Use z with the Z table to find a probability.

2.2.3.d.title: Normality tests
2.2.3.d.html: Common tests: Anderson-Darling (the Minitab default), Shapiro-Wilk, Ryan-Joiner, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov. They all share the same logic.

2.2.3.e.title: Interpreting the p-value
2.2.3.e.html:
H0: the data are normal.

  • p ≤ 0.05: evidence against normality.
  • p > 0.05: fail to reject H0. That is not proof of normality.

Also look at the probability plot. Small samples have little power to detect non-normality, and very large samples flag deviations too small to matter.

2.2.3.f.title: The normal probability plot
2.2.3.f.html: The points should fall close to a straight line, within the confidence bands, if the data are normal. Curves and S-shapes signal skew or heavy tails.

2.2.3.g.title: Reasons data are not normal
2.2.3.g.html: Skewed processes, mixed populations (two machines or shifts blended), outliers, bounded data (cannot go below zero), and coarse rounding.

2.2.3.h.title: "p = 0.02 on the normality test"
2.2.3.h.html: Data are not normal at α = 0.05. Memory aid: low p, null must go.

2.2.3.i.title: Failing to reject is not proof
2.2.3.i.html: A large p-value does not show the data are normal, and the answer depends on sample size.

2.2.3.j.title: Reading the Z table
2.2.3.j.html:
The reference document (version 1.4.2) has two Z tables.

  • Left Tail Area, for Z from −4.9 to 0.0, gives P(Z below z). Example: Z = −1.96 gives 0.02500.
  • A second table, titled "Right Tail Area," covers Z from 0.00 to 4.9 but actually lists the area to the left of Z (0.50000 at Z = 0.00, and 0.97500 at Z = 1.96).

So P(Z above z) = 1 − (table value for z), or read the left-tail table at −z. P(Z between −z and z) = 2 × (table value for z) − 1.
Examples: P(Z above 1.00) = 1 − 0.84134 = 0.15866. P(Z between −1 and 1) = 2 × 0.84134 − 1 = 0.6827.

2.2.3.k.title: Table limits
2.2.3.k.html: The Z table stops at Z = 4.9, and very small tails print as 0.00000. For 6σ-level questions, expect the known value (3.4 DPMO) rather than a table lookup.

2.2.4.a.title: Histogram
2.2.4.a.html: Shows the shape, center, and spread of continuous data. The number of bins matters: too few hides detail, too many looks like noise. Shapes include symmetric, skewed, and bimodal.

2.2.4.b.title: Boxplot
2.2.4.b.html: The box runs from Q1 to Q3, with a line at the median. Whiskers extend to the most extreme points within 1.5 × IQR, and points beyond are plotted as outliers. Boxplots are ideal for comparing groups side by side. A median near one edge of the box signals skew.

2.2.4.c.title: Other displays
2.2.4.c.html:
• Dotplot and individual value plot: show each data point, good for small samples.
  • Interval plot: shows a confidence interval for each group's mean.
  • Stem-and-leaf: a text-based histogram that keeps the actual values.

2.2.4.d.title: Run chart
2.2.4.d.html: Plots data in time order. It shows trends, shifts, cycles, and oscillation. Use it to see how a process behaves over time.

2.2.4.e.title: Scatterplot
2.2.4.e.html: Plots two continuous variables against each other to show a relationship: positive, negative, none, or curved.

2.2.4.f.title: Normal probability plot and Pareto chart
2.2.4.f.html: The normal probability plot checks normality (2.2.3.f). The Pareto chart ranks categories by frequency or cost (1.2.4).

2.2.4.g.title: A bimodal histogram
2.2.4.g.html: Two peaks usually mean two populations are mixed together (two machines, two shifts, two suppliers). The fix is to separate (stratify) the data and analyze each group.

2.2.4.h.title: Which chart?
2.2.4.h.html:
• Compare groups: boxplot or interval plot.
  • Behavior over time: run chart.
  • Relationship between two variables: scatterplot.
  • Shape of one variable's distribution: histogram.
  • Which categories matter most: Pareto chart.

2.2.1-1.stem: Which of the following is continuous data?

options.html: The number of defects on a panel
Pass or fail on an inspection
The time, in seconds, to answer a call
The shift on which a unit was made

2.2.1-1.explanation: Time is measured and can take any value. The others are counts or categories.

2.2.1-2.stem: Events A and B are independent, with P(A) = 0.40 and P(B) = 0.25. What are P(A and B) and P(A or B)?

2.2.1-3.stem: Two mutually exclusive events that each have a positive probability are also independent.
2.2.1-3.explanation: If one occurs, the other cannot, so knowing one tells you about the other. They are dependent.

2.2.2-1.stem: A sample has the values 6, 8, 10, 12, and 14. What is the sample standard deviation?
2.2.2-1.explanation: Mean = 10. Squared deviations: 16, 4, 0, 4, 16, total 40. Sample variance = 40 ÷ 4 = 10, so s = 3.16. The value 2.83 is the population standard deviation (40 ÷ 5 = 8).

2.2.2-2.stem: A data set has a mean of 52 and a median of 48. What does this suggest?
2.2.2-2.explanation: The mean is pulled above the median by a long right tail, which is right (positive) skew.

2.2.2-3.stem: Two independent parts are stacked. Their standard deviations are 6 and 8. What is the standard deviation of the stack?
2.2.2-3.explanation: Variances add: 36 + 64 = 100, so the standard deviation is 10. Standard deviations do not add directly.

2.2.2-4.stem: A student scores 70 on a test weighted 2 and 90 on a test weighted 3. What is the weighted mean?

2.2.3-1.stem: A process is normal with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 5. What fraction of output exceeds 110?
2.2.3-1.explanation: z = (110 − 100) ÷ 5 = 2.0. The area beyond 2.0 is 0.02275, about 2.3%. On the sheet: 1 − 0.97725, or the left-tail table at −2.00.

2.2.3-2.stem: An Anderson-Darling normality test returns p = 0.003. What do you conclude at α = 0.05?

options.html: There is evidence the data are not normal

2.2.3-2.explanation: p is below 0.05, so there is evidence against normality. Memory aid: low p, null must go.

2.2.3-3.stem: A normality test p-value of 0.40 proves the data are normal.
2.2.3-3.explanation: A large p-value means you failed to find evidence against normality. It is not proof, and small samples have little power to detect non-normality.

2.2.3-4.stem: Using the Z tables in the Reference Document, the probability that Z falls between −1.96 and 1.96 is closest to:
2.2.3-4.explanation: The positive table gives 0.97500 at Z = 1.96. The left-tail table gives 0.02500 at Z = −1.96. The difference is 0.95.

2.2.3-5.stem: A histogram of cycle times shows two distinct peaks. What is the most likely explanation?

options.html: Two different processes or sources are mixed in the data

2.2.3-5.explanation: Two peaks usually mean two populations (two machines, shifts, or suppliers) are blended together.

2.2.4-1.stem: Which chart is best for comparing cycle times across three shifts?
2.2.4-1.explanation: Boxplots compare the center and spread of several groups side by side.

2.2.4-2.stem: Which TWO displays are used to show how a process behaves over time?
2.2.4-2.explanation: Run charts and control charts plot data in time order. A histogram shows distribution shape, not time behavior.

2.2.4-3.stem: A team wants to see whether oven temperature is related to defect rate. Which chart should they use first?
2.2.4-3.explanation: A scatterplot shows the relationship between two continuous variables.
